title: Lesson 22: Building Repeatable Processes: Checklists, Templates, and a Delivery Framework v1
description: Building the three assets a practice compounds on: checklists that catch real failures, templates that capture decision history, and a delivery framework with gates, extracted from real engagements and versioned.

questions.question: What makes a strong checklist item?
options: A broad reminder that restates the plan for the current phase
A step that has failed before and fails silently when it is dropped
A long list that covers every task in the framework from start to finish
A description of the desired outcome rather than any specific step
questions.explanation: A checklist is a pre-mortem device, not a to-do list. It names the high-consequence step whose failure is silent and should stay short enough to be consulted under pressure.

questions.question: What distinguishes a useful template from a blank form?
options: It has more fields and longer sections for the next person to fill in
It is stored in a shared tool that the whole team can reach at once
Each field carries the reasoning a past engagement learned to ask
It is reviewed and approved by the client before the engagement begins
questions.explanation: A blank form gives boxes with no guidance, while a real template encodes the questions earlier work paid to discover. That captured reasoning is what makes it transferable and worth versioning.

questions.question: What turns a sequence of phases into a repeatable, priceable delivery framework?
options: Defined outputs and gates before work moves to the next phase
A detailed timeline that lists every task in chronological order
A flexible plan the consultant reinvents for each new client engagement
A fixed method that is never revised once it has been written down
questions.explanation: Gates are where variation gets caught early and where a failure becomes cheap and visible. A known process with known outputs is estimable and priceable in a way an improvisation is not.
